title: Unpaired Value in a Sorted List
statement:
You get a sorted array nums in which every value appears exactly twice, side by side, except one value that appears only once. Return that value.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time and O(1) extra space. A linear scan or XOR over everything is correct but too slow for what is asked.

examples.why: Before the 4, pairs start at even indexes (0). After it, pairs start at odd indexes (3, 5). The lone value is where that switch happens.
The lone value can be the last element. A search that only looks between two pairs never finds it.
A single element is the answer itself.

constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 100 000, and the length is odd
nums is sorted; every value but one appears exactly twice
hints: Look at the index where each pair starts, before and after the lone value. What changes?
Before the lone value, every pair starts at an even index. After it, every pair starts at an odd index. So the array is split into a "good" left part and a "shifted" right part.
Binary search on even indexes only: if nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1], the pairing is still intact up to mid, so search right of mid + 1; otherwise the lone value is at mid or to its left.

explain.intuition:
The values themselves are not what you search on. The positions are. In a perfect paired array, each pair sits at indexes (0, 1), (2, 3), (4, 5) … so the first copy of every pair is at an even index. The lone value pushes everything after it one step to the right, so from then on the first copy sits at an odd index.

That gives a yes/no question you can ask at any even index mid: "does nums[mid] still equal nums[mid + 1]?" Yes means the lone value is further right. No means it is at mid or before. A monotone yes/no question is exactly what binary search needs.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = n − 1. The answer is always in [lo, hi], and both stay at even indexes.
While lo < hi: take mid = (lo + hi) / 2, and if it is odd, subtract one so it is even.
If nums[mid] === nums[mid + 1], the pairs are intact through mid + 1, so set lo = mid + 2.
Otherwise set hi = mid: the lone value is at mid or earlier.
pitfalls: Comparing with the neighbour without fixing parity first. At an odd mid, "equals the next one" means the opposite.
Setting hi = mid − 1 when the pair is broken. Mid itself may be the lone value.
Searching on values (like the middle value) instead of on index parity. The values give no hint about which half holds the lone one.

solutions.title: Step through the pairs
solutions.idea: Walk in steps of two and return the first position whose neighbour is different. Simple, but linear.

solutions.title: Binary search on even indexes
solutions.idea: At an even index the pair is intact exactly when the lone value is further right. Search for the first broken pair.

followups: The array is not sorted, but equal values are still adjacent. Does the same search still work?
Every value appears exactly three times in a row except one. How does the parity trick change?
